chapters.summary: This chapter records the LORD's instructions to Moses concerning the burnt offering, stressing that the one offering it must bring an animal without blemish and present it according to the prescribed ritual.
keyPoints: The burnt offering could be taken from the herd, the flock, or the birds, but it had to be without blemish.
The offerer laid a hand on the animal's head to identify with it and make atonement, then slaughtered it.
The priest sprinkled the blood on the altar and burned the whole offering as a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.
chapters.application: We should offer ourselves to God wholeheartedly, holding nothing back, just as the burnt offering was consumed entirely, living out holiness and obedience in our daily lives.

chapters.summary: This chapter details the regulations for the grain offering, including fine flour, unleavened cakes, and firstfruits, emphasizing sincerity and gratitude in worship.
keyPoints: The grain offering was made of fine flour with oil and frankincense, burned on the altar as a pleasing aroma.
Unleavened cakes were mixed or anointed with oil but never with leaven, since leaven symbolized sin.
Firstfruits were offered as roasted grain in thanksgiving, with a reminder of the everlasting covenant of salt.
chapters.application: What we offer to God is not merely material but a sincere heart. Gratitude and obedience in everyday life rise before him like a pleasing aroma, acceptable in his sight.

chapters.summary: This chapter describes the regulations for the peace offering, emphasizing reconciliation with God and the shared joy of the offering.
keyPoints: An unblemished ox was presented as a peace offering, with a hand laid on its head before it was slaughtered at the entrance of the tabernacle.
The priest burned the fat and inner parts on the altar as a pleasing aroma, a food offering to the LORD.
Sheep or goats offered as peace offerings likewise had to be without blemish; the fat belonged to God, and the blood was never to be eaten.
chapters.application: Let us be reconciled to God with a thankful heart, share joyfully in his grace, and obey his commands, living out a holy life.

chapters.summary: This chapter records the LORD's instructions to Moses concerning the sin offering for unintentional sin, prescribing different offerings and rituals depending on the offender's standing — anointed priest, whole congregation, leader, or common person.
keyPoints: Unintentional sin required a sin offering, with the procedure varying according to the offender's standing.
When the priest offered on behalf of the anointed priest or the whole congregation, the blood was brought into the tabernacle.
When a leader or a common person offered, the blood was put on the horns of the altar and the rest poured out at its base.
chapters.application: We may sin without meaning to, yet God has provided a way of forgiveness. Let us come with a humble, repentant heart, trusting in the blood of Christ for cleansing and living a holy life.

chapters.summary: This chapter covers the regulations for the guilt offering, addressing various kinds of unintentional sin and their offerings, with an emphasis on confession and restitution.
keyPoints: Failing to testify or unknowingly touching something unclean still incurred guilt, even without awareness.
After sinning, a person had to confess the wrong and bring a guilt offering.
The offering was scaled to one's means — the poor could bring turtledoves or fine flour — showing God's grace.
chapters.application: We often sin without realizing it, yet God calls us to examine ourselves and confess. He is mindful of our weakness and provides a way suited to what we can bear — we need only come before him freely.

chapters.summary: This chapter continues the regulations for the guilt offering, stressing that restitution and sacrifice go together, and sets out the priests' duties and their portion of the offerings.
keyPoints: Anyone who wronged a neighbor had to make full restitution plus a fifth, and then bring a guilt offering.
The priest kept the fire burning on the altar and tended it so the burnt offering was consumed completely.
The most holy portions of the grain offering, sin offering, and guilt offering belonged to the priests, to be eaten in a holy place.
chapters.application: When we wrong someone, we must not only confess to God but also make right what we owe them, showing that our repentance is genuine.

chapters.summary: This chapter details further regulations for the guilt offering and the peace offering, along with the priest's rightful portion and other matters to observe when sacrificing.
keyPoints: The procedure for the guilt offering and the priest's allotted portion are set out.
The peace offering had different requirements depending on whether it was for thanksgiving, a vow, or a freewill gift.
Eating blood or the fat of sacrificial animals was forbidden, on penalty of being cut off from the people.
chapters.application: In everyday life, let us live with a thankful heart, offer God our very best, and carefully keep his commands, living out a holy and obedient life.

chapters.summary: This chapter records how Moses, following the LORD's command, ordained Aaron and his sons as priests, setting them apart and consecrating them to their sacred office.
keyPoints: Moses gathered the whole congregation at the entrance of the tabernacle and proclaimed that the ordination would follow God's own instructions.
Aaron and his sons were washed, clothed in priestly garments, and anointed, symbolizing cleansing and consecration.
A sin offering, a burnt offering, and the ram of ordination were offered, with blood sprinkled and oil applied to complete the ceremony.
chapters.application: Though we are not priests, God also calls us to live holy lives, offering ourselves to him each day and serving faithfully wherever he has placed us, for his glory.

chapters.summary: After Aaron was ordained to the priesthood, he offered sacrifices as the LORD commanded, and the glory of the LORD appeared, showing that he accepted their service.
keyPoints: Moses instructed Aaron to prepare the offerings and present a sin offering and a burnt offering on behalf of the people.
Aaron blessed the people, and when he and Moses entered the tabernacle, the glory of the LORD appeared to all.
Fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the offering, and the people shouted for joy and fell facedown.
chapters.application: Our service should follow God's own instructions, and he will accept it and confirm his presence with us. May we live with reverence and behold his glory in our daily lives.

chapters.summary: Aaron's sons were struck down by the LORD for offering unauthorized fire, and Moses taught the priests to serve with great care, along with regulations concerning sacrifice and purity.
keyPoints: Aaron's sons Nadab and Abihu offered unauthorized fire before the LORD and were consumed by fire from him.
Moses explained that God's holiness requires the priests to be careful and set apart when drawing near to him.
The priests were forbidden to mourn for the dead in the ordinary way, and were told to honor God as holy and keep the dietary regulations.
chapters.application: In our life of faith, we should serve God with reverence, never acting on our own impulse, but obeying his commands and honoring him as holy.

chapters.summary: This chapter records the LORD's instructions to Moses and Aaron concerning clean and unclean animals, teaching the Israelites to distinguish which creatures could be eaten and which could not.
keyPoints: Clear distinctions were drawn between clean and unclean land animals, fish, birds, and crawling creatures.
The call to holy living was emphasized, since God is holy, and his chosen people were to be set apart even in what they ate.

Specific prohibitions were listed, such as animals that chewed the cud but did not have a split hoof, or creatures without fins and scales, along with instructions for becoming clean after touching something unclean.
chapters.application: Though we today are not bound by the Old Testament dietary laws, we should learn to obey God in every area of life, pursuing holiness and living lives set apart from the world.

chapters.summary: God instructed Moses concerning the purification of a woman after childbirth, including sacrifice and a period of separation, to address the uncleanness that came with bearing a child.
keyPoints: A woman who bore a son was unclean for seven days, and the child was circumcised on the eighth day.
A woman who bore a daughter was unclean for two weeks and remained at home for sixty-six days.
At the end of the purification period she offered a burnt offering and a sin offering, and the priest made atonement for her.
chapters.application: God cares about every detail of our lives, including childbirth. Let us receive his laws with a grateful heart and rely on his forgiveness and cleansing.

chapters.summary: This chapter details how the priest was to examine and handle skin diseases on the body and mildew on clothing, in order to keep the Israelite camp clean.
keyPoints: The priest examined anyone with a suspected defiling skin disease and quarantined them for seven days of observation.
If the condition spread or persisted, the person was declared unclean and had to live alone outside the camp.
Mildew on clothing also had to be examined, and the distinction between clean and unclean showed how seriously God takes holiness.
chapters.application: Though we no longer live under this law, God still wants us to value inward purity, and to receive those who are isolated with love and wisdom.

chapters.summary: This chapter records the rituals for cleansing a person healed of a defiling skin disease, including priestly examination and sacrifice, along with how to handle mildew in a house, emphasizing God's demand for cleanness and holiness.
keyPoints: Once healed, a person had to be examined by the priest and bring a guilt offering, a sin offering, and a burnt offering to be declared clean.
The cleansing ritual involved sprinkling blood seven times using running water, cedar wood, scarlet thread, and hyssop, symbolizing thorough cleansing.
A house with a spreading mildew was shut up for seven days; if the mildew spread it was torn down, but if it cleared, a cleansing ritual was performed.
chapters.application: We should examine the 'defiling disease' in our own lives — sin and impurity — and be cleansed through the blood of Christ, living holy lives that bring glory to God.

chapters.summary: This chapter sets out the regulations for cleansing from bodily discharges in both men and women, showing the link between physical cleanliness and holy living.
keyPoints: Anyone with a discharge was to be isolated, and anything they touched became unclean and had to be washed or burned.
Once healed of a discharge, a person offered a sin offering and a burnt offering to be made clean before the LORD.
Regulations also covered the uncleanness of sexual relations and a woman's monthly period, along with the required cleansing.
chapters.application: We should attend to the impurity in our own lives, cleansing ourselves through prayer and God's word, pursuing holiness and drawing near to him each day.

chapters.summary: This chapter records the regulations for the Day of Atonement, including the high priest's sacrifices, the atonement made, and the cleansing of the sanctuary, so that the people's sins were forgiven.
keyPoints: The high priest first had to offer a sin offering for himself and his household before he could make atonement for the people.
Two male goats were chosen: one was sacrificed to the LORD as a sin offering, and the other was sent away into the wilderness to Azazel, bearing the people's sins.
On the Day of Atonement the people were to deny themselves, an everlasting statute by which they were made clean.
chapters.application: Today we no longer need to offer sacrifices, because Christ offered himself once for all. Let us respond with gratitude, turn away from sin, and live holy lives.

chapters.summary: This chapter regulates where and how the Israelites were to sacrifice, emphasizing that life is in the blood, forbidding the eating of blood, and requiring that every offering be brought to the entrance of the tabernacle.
keyPoints: Any Israelite who slaughtered an ox or a sheep had to bring it to the entrance of the tabernacle to offer it, or else be guilty of bloodshed.
Sacrificing to demons, that is, to goat idols, was forbidden, and anyone who did so was to be cut off from the people.
The prohibition against eating blood applied to everyone, since life is in the blood, and it is the blood that makes atonement.
chapters.application: Let us worship God with reverence, honor the value of life, keep far from idols, and live holy lives in our everyday walk.

chapters.summary: This chapter records God's laws through Moses concerning sexual morality and forbidden practices against one's neighbor, stressing that Israel was to be holy and not imitate the evil customs of Egypt and Canaan.
keyPoints: The LORD instructed Moses that Israel was to keep his statutes and ordinances, and not follow the evil practices of Egypt and Canaan.
Various forbidden acts were detailed in depth, including incest, homosexual relations, and bestiality.
A warning was given that those who committed these detestable acts would be cut off from the people, and that the land itself would vomit out its inhabitants.
chapters.application: Let us fear God, keep far from every impurity and worldly temptation, and honor the holiness of our bodies, for our bodies are the temple of the Holy Spirit.

chapters.summary: This chapter reaffirms God's demand for holiness, teaching the Israelites through specific laws how to love their neighbor, keep the Sabbath, and worship God.
keyPoints: 'Be holy, because I the LORD your God am holy' stands at the heart of this chapter's command.
The people were not to steal, deceive, or lie, but to treat their neighbors and hired workers fairly.
They were to love their neighbor as themselves, not take revenge or bear a grudge, and judge with justice.
chapters.application: In daily life, let us treat others with reverence for God, be honest and fair, take the initiative to care for those in need, and live as witnesses of love.

chapters.summary: This chapter reaffirms the severe penalties for offering children to Molech, consulting mediums, and practicing sorcery, and emphasizes that Israel was to be set apart and keep God's statutes.
keyPoints: Anyone who gave a child to Molech was to be put to death by stoning and cut off from the people.
Anyone who turned to mediums and spiritists would have God set his face against them and cut them off from the people.
The laws of sexual morality were reaffirmed, with punishment for violation, so that the people would be holy.
chapters.application: Today let us keep far from every idol and occult practice, hold fast to a holy life, and fear God, for he is holy and calls us to be holy as well.

chapters.summary: This chapter requires the priests to keep themselves holy, avoiding defilement through contact with the dead and physical blemishes, in order to preserve the sanctity of their office.
keyPoints: A priest was not to touch a dead body or mourn for anyone outside his immediate family, so as not to defile his sacred office.
Priests were not to shave their heads, trim the edges of their beards, or cut their bodies, but were to be holy to God and never profane his name.
A priest with a physical defect could not come near to offer sacrifices, though he could still eat the holy food, out of respect for God's holiness.
chapters.application: Though we are not priests, we too are called to be saints, and should respond to God's call with holy living, honoring him in word and deed.

chapters.summary: This chapter reaffirms the requirement of holiness for priests and people regarding sacred things, emphasizing that God's name must not be profaned and that offerings must be without blemish.
keyPoints: Priests were to keep themselves from uncleanness so as not to profane the holy things.
Only priests who were clean, along with their households, could eat the holy food.
Offerings had to be without blemish; no animal with a defect could be presented.
chapters.application: In our daily lives, let us treat what God has given us with reverence and offer him our very best, never with carelessness or half-heartedness.

chapters.summary: This chapter sets out in detail the appointed feasts of Israel, including the Sabbath, Passover, the Feast of Weeks, and the Feast of Tabernacles, as sacred assemblies and times of offering.
keyPoints: The LORD instructed Moses to proclaim the appointed feasts to Israel, with the Sabbath as their foundation.
Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread commemorated the exodus from Egypt, with unleavened bread and food offerings presented.
The Feast of Weeks brought an offering of firstfruits, and the Feast of Tabernacles recalled Israel's time dwelling in the wilderness, forming a yearly cycle of worship.
chapters.application: In our busy lives, let us set aside time to draw near to God, remember his salvation and provision, and worship him with gratitude and joy.

chapters.summary: This chapter records the regulations for the lampstand and the bread of the Presence in the sanctuary, along with the case of a man executed for blasphemy, and reaffirms the principle of just retribution.
keyPoints: The people were instructed to bring pure olive oil so the lamp could be kept burning continually, symbolizing God's presence.
Twelve loaves of bread were to be set out every Sabbath as an everlasting covenant.
The son of an Israelite woman blasphemed the Name and was brought before Moses, then stoned to death as the LORD had commanded.
chapters.application: Let us worship God with reverence, watch our words, never take his name in vain, and trust in his righteous judgment, living holy lives each day.

chapters.summary: God instituted the Sabbatical year and the Year of Jubilee, requiring the Israelites to let the land rest, free their slaves, restore property, and trust in his provision.
keyPoints: Every seventh year was a Sabbatical year, when the land was to rest and go unplanted, its yield left for the poor, the animals, and the wild creatures.
The fiftieth year was the Year of Jubilee, announced with a trumpet blast on the Day of Atonement, when everyone returned to their family and their land was restored to its original owner.
Land was not to be sold permanently, since it belonged to the LORD; anyone whose brother grew poor was to help him without charging interest, out of reverence for God.
chapters.application: Let us trust in God's provision, learn to rest regularly, care for the poor, and hold fast to fairness and mercy, so that our lives display God's grace and justice.

chapters.summary: God promised blessing for obedience and warned of punishment for rebellion, but ultimately promised restoration for those who repent.
keyPoints: The people were not to worship idols but were to keep the Sabbath and fear God.
Obedience would bring rain, abundant harvest, peace, and God's presence.
Rebellion would bring disaster, but after repentance, God would remember his covenant.
chapters.application: Today let us obey God's word wholeheartedly, and even when we stumble and fall, let us turn back quickly, trusting firmly in his grace and mercy.

chapters.summary: This chapter concerns the regulations for vows, including the valuation and redemption of persons, animals, houses, and fields, along with the rules for the tithe.
keyPoints: A vow or dedication was valued according to a set scale, with a person's worth assessed by age and sex.
Firstborn animals already belonged to the LORD and could not be vowed again; redeeming a vowed animal required paying its value plus a fifth.
Houses and fields could be redeemed, but if permanently dedicated they belonged to the priests as holy.
chapters.application: Our giving should come from a willing heart, and we should keep our promises. God values the sincerity within us; may we offer ourselves to him with gratitude.
